newsitem.title: CANADA: ADM deal with UGG seen with eye on Wheat Board.
newsitem.headline: ADM deal with UGG seen with eye on Wheat Board.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co's decision to acquire a 45 percent stake in Canada's second largest grain handler was likely done with an eye on the fate of the Canadian Wheat Board, grain industry analysts said.
"This is obviously some long-term planning. They're assuming they won't have to deal with the Canadian Wheat Board in five or 10 years," said University of Manitoba agriculture economist Daryl Kraft.
United Grain Growers Ltd announced the C$113 million (US$82 million) deal with Decatur, Illinois-based ADM on Thursday, the latest in a string of merger deals for ADM.
"Clearly, they'd like to control the grain without having to negotiate with an intermediary," Kraft said.

The Canadian Wheat Board -- a state trading company with a monopoly on exports of barley and wheat from Western Canada -- has been under attack in recent years from many quarters, including Canadian farmers, competing grain companies like UGG, U.S. farm lobbies and one political party aiming to form Canada's next federal government in Monday's national vote.
"We see the Canadian industry becoming less regulated and more dynamic," UGG president Ted Allen said. "This alliance gives us a link to one of the biggest end users in the world."
The ADM deal is subject to a shareholder vote July 17.

"Our decisions are based on the current business environment," ADM vice-president Martin Andreas told reporters on Thursday. "We're interested in doing more processing in Canada. We think there's going to be considerable growth in exports."
More than 20,000 farmers voted to strike down the CWB's single-desk monopoly sales of barley in a plebiscite in March, but 63 percent of the 57,000 voters voted to retain the CWB.
CWB opponents have said they will continue pressure for the option to sell grain outside traditional CWB channels.

Such winds of change have attracted more U.S. agribusiness giants than ADM, analysts said. Omaha-based grain miller ConAgra Inc began building four elevators in Western Canada in October. Cargill Inc and ADM both crush canola now.
As of last July, UGG owned 173 primary elevators in western Canada, down from 220 facilities a year earlier. The elevators handled 5.5 million tonnes of grain a year.

ADM owns, leases or has a 50 percent or greater interest in 276 processing plants including 40 oilseed crushing plants worldwide, two of which are in Canada. It also has 17 oilseed refineries, two in Canada, and 32 flour mills, 10 in Canada.
ADM also has four barley malting plants in the U.S. and one in Canada.
"UGG is an attractive partner for us in western Canada," ADM chief executive officer Allen Andreas said. "The company has some of the most modern and efficient grain handling facilities in Canada."
The ADM deal will result in about C$50 million in net new capital for UGG to apply to capital expenses on its grain handling facilities, the companies said.
"This is a natural strategic fit between out two companies," UGG's Allen said.
The ADM stake also comes after a bitter, hostile and unsuccessful takeover bid for UGG by Alberta Wheat Pool and Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, withdrawn on March 18.
